newsitem.title: UK: UK tobacco industry urges Labour government to talk.
newsitem.headline: UK tobacco industry urges Labour government to talk.

text.p: Britain's tobacco industry has urged the newly elected Labour Party to talk first before implementing its promise to ban tobacco advertising, saying it is unclear what it means by advertising.

All three domestic cigarette makers -- Gallaher, Rothmans, owned by Cie Financire Richemont AG, and Imperial Tobacco -- are calling on government to talk about their plans first and to take into account existing restrictions under a voluntary code.

"We obviously hope they don't do anything, but we're realistic enough to know that they have made a comitment in their manifesto and as far as we know they intend to keep it," John Carlisle, executive director for industry affairs at the Tobacco Manufacturers Association, said on Tuesday.

"We obviously want to have discussions with the government. I think any industry would want that. Our door is open and hopefully their door is open, too," he said. "We don't fully know what the Labour government has in mind."

The British industry currently spends about 50 million pounds ($80 million) a year on advertising and is banned from advertising cigarettes on television and radio under a voluntary agreement, signed with the government two years ago, which expires in July 1999.

All the major tobacco importers into Britain, like R.J. Reynolds, are also party to the agreement. It prohibits the use of billboards within 200 metres of schools, and ads must not appeal to children in any way.
No permanent external advertising outside shops is allowed and there are limits on total industry expenditure allowed on poster campaigns.
At the end of 1997 no ads for cigarettes or hand rolling tobacco will be permitted on the outside of any public vehicle or vehicles owned by tobacco firms.

Cigarette companies are also no longer allowed small poster advertising and 20 percent of any billboard ad must include health warnings. The companies can, however, advertise cigars and pipe tobacco in cinemas and on radio.
Tobacco manufacturers also agreed to spend more on advertising low tar products like Silk Cut.
"It may be they are talking about a complete ban on billboards. That's why we need discussion," said Paul Sadler, head of external affairs at Imperial Tobacco.
Imperial, owners of the Lambert and Butler and Embassy brands, have about 38 percent of the British market.

Ian Birks, general manager of corporate affairs at Gallaher, which is owned by American Brands Inc, said: "I am not exactly sure what they mean by an advertising ban. I understand it as TV, radio and cinema but there maybe some others in their sights."
Cigarette companies also appeal to smokers through poster campaigns, newspapers, magazines, sports sponsorship, loyalty schemes and direct mail.
Gallaher, which has written to health minister Frank Dobson requesting a meeting, is the market leader in Britain with some 40 percent of sales, selling 32 billion cigarettes a year.
The company's premium brands in Britain include Benson and Hedges and Silk Cut as well as lower priced brands Sovereign and Mayfair.
Many analysts think further restrictions on tobacco advertising will cause smokers to drop their brand loyalty in favour of cheaper brands.

Sales of premium brands like Benson and Hedges at around 3.12 pounds ($5.04) a packet have already suffered from heavy and successive increases in excise duty as smokers shift to cheaper brands like Mayfair at 2.57 pounds for 20.
"I think a complete ban would erode the sales of B&H and the like but they may make it up on savings in ad spend," said Panmure Gordon analyst John Nuttall. ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
